title: [Chapitre] VIII. Analysis situs (quatrième mouture) : notes manuscrites (26/06-04/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 90-92). L is a totally ordered set (an abstract 'line'). M is the set of 'cells' over L: points P_a (a in L) and closed segments S_{a,b} (a<b). Figures are finite unions of cells. For a nonempty finite chain ('drapeau') T = {a_0<...<a_n} in L, F_T is the connected figure made of the points P_{a_i} and the segments S_{a_i,a_{i+1}}. The previous page proves two things. First, the F_T for T in a set 𝒯 of flags are pairwise disjoint iff 𝒯 is itself a chain in the ordered set Drap*(L). Second, T ↦ F_T gives a bijection Drap(Drap*(L)) → Fig fin(M), sending a flag of flags to its disjoint union. Connected components are recovered combinatorially.

This page opens with a picture of such a figure: segments with interior ticks, interleaved with isolated points. The caption notes that the connected components 'follow one another' in the order of L.

Grothendieck then wants to determine the 'elements' (cells) of a figure intrinsically. For this he introduces hypotheses on L. Hypothesis H is a struck-through and rewritten clause about minimal elements: no smaller element below a non-minimal point. Hypothesis b) is density of L. Both are needed already for Lemma 1.

A crossed-out first Lemma 1 concerned two cells X, Y in the relation X||Y, with Φ ⊂ Omb X and Ψ ⊂ Omb Y; it claimed Supp°(Φ∪Ψ) = Supp°(Φ). The surviving Lemma 1 says: for a cell X, supp(X) := supp°(X̃) equals Omb(X) = {Y in M : |Y| ⊂ |X|}, the 'shadow' of X, i.e. its closed subcells. The inclusion Omb ⊂ supp is called trivial; the reverse less so.

From the next page, supp° is a bi-orthogonal (double 'cosupport') closure with respect to a disjointness-type relation |∘| between cells. So Lemma 1 says: the polar closure of a single cell is exactly its set of faces and subcells. A margin defines the open version Omb°(X) = {Y : |Y| ⊊ |X|}, apparently with supp°(X) = Omb°(X). The next page specialises: Supp{P_a} = {P_a}, and Supp{S_{a,b}} = all points and subsegments of [a,b].

A rotated left-margin note sketches an 'other possibility' for the axiomatics. A figure (or 'variété') F would come with boundary ∂F = ∪T = F_0, plus a partition into interiors Int T of cells, with dimension data. This is essentially a stratified or CW-type description.

Purpose: build a purely order-theoretic / combinatorial 1-dimensional 'analysis situs' (tame topology). In it, cells and their incidences are recovered from a lattice of 'supports' defined by orthogonality, as a step toward the higher-dimensional theory of the quatrième mouture.
errors: Hypothesis H as legible ('if L has no smallest element, then for every a in L there exists x in L with x < a') is a tautology, the definition of 'no smallest element'. The intended hypothesis is unclear from the struck-through text. Since the next page explicitly treats the case where a is a smallest or largest element, endpoints are allowed; the real content seems to be the density hypothesis b).

The relation symbols (||, |∘|) and the notation X̃ are not defined on this page. The equality supp°(X) = Omb°(X) in the margin is stated without proof and must depend on density. In a non-dense L, a segment S_{a,b} with nothing strictly between a and b would presumably not be separated by orthogonality, so the lemma needs hypothesis b).

ideas.what: Classification of finite figures on an ordered line by flags of flags (connected components = chains, ordered linearly)
ideas.modern_name: combinatorial 1-dimensional cell complexes / definable subsets of an ordered set (o-minimal cell decomposition in dimension 1)
ideas.usually_credited_to: o-minimality: van den Dries, Pillay-Steinhorn (1984-86); folklore for dimension 1
ideas.where_published: Programme of 'topologie modérée' announced in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), without such details

ideas.what: Recovering the cells under a cell as a bi-orthogonal (polar) closure: supp(X) = Omb(X)
ideas.modern_name: Galois connection / polarity closure (Birkhoff), orthogonality closure

ideas.what: Density hypothesis on L needed for the intrinsic determination of cells
ideas.modern_name: dense linear order (DLO), the basic o-minimal structure

ideas.what: Alternative axiomatics: figure with boundary plus partition into open cells by dimension
ideas.modern_name: stratified spaces / regular CW complexes / tame stratifications
ideas.usually_credited_to: Whitney, Thom, Mather; Grothendieck's 'tame topology' programme
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme §5 discusses tame topology in general terms

missed.claim: Grothendieck tries to recover the cell structure of 'figures' over an arbitrary ordered set purely from an orthogonality/support closure. This is an order-theoretic foundation for tame topology, distinct from the model-theoretic o-minimal approach. The 1-dimensional case is worked out; the general axiomatics (margin 'Autre possibilité') is only sketched.
missed.quote: Lemme 1 Soit X ∈ M. Alors supp(X) (=def supp°(X̃)) = Omb(X) = {Y ∈ M | |Y| ⊂ |X|}
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a possible lattice-theoretic route to Grothendieck's tame topology, comparable with o-minimal cell decomposition and with point-free approaches. It has received little or no treatment in the literature, though this page itself is elementary.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics on this page is elementary: a Galois-closure lemma for cells on a dense line. It is mainly of historical interest as part of Grothendieck's unpublished combinatorial tame-topology project of 1986.
transcription_corrections: 'b) hypothèse dense' is more likely 'b) hypothèse densité' (or 'de densité').
The phrase after 'se suivent :' is probably an ordinal enumeration of the components ('la première - la deuxième - ...'), not 'le premier - leur - leur'.
The insertion above Hypothèse H reads roughly 'si L a élément minimal de L' rather than '$T$ a élément minimal de $L$'.
The first segment of the struck-through Lemma 1 margin is 'X ‖ Y'; the subsets read 'Φ ⊂ Omb X, Ψ ⊂ Omb Y'.
In the bottom-left margin, 'supp°(X) = Omb°(X) =def {Y ∈ M | |Y| ⊊ |X|}' (proper inclusion) is correctly read.
